notes.key_messages: This paper was mainly assessed for writing, although there were ten marks available for reading in Question 1 . The requirements for doing well were to: ● write with a specific audience in mind and adapt content and style to that audience ● structure each answer overall and sequence sentences in well-formed, individual paragraphs ● create cogent and effective arguments and present descriptions and stories that were credible, original and engaging in their content ● write in a variety of well-formed sentence types, including complex sentences ● use a wide range of effective and appropriate vocabulary.
notes.general_comments: This paper was frequently well answered. The writing was often fluent, engaging and varied and there was an awareness of the requirements set by the mark scheme, which remains the same from session to session with the exception of content for the Reading mark scheme. The general standard was high and the following general comments are designed to show where improvements for subsequent sessions can be made. While Question 1 was often well answered, there were responses that needed to move beyond summarising the arguments. These responses tended to begin with a focused introduction that showed general understanding of the debate and a closing rallying call for the readers of the article to ‘do their part’. Less successful summaries gathered a group of basic points for one group and then did exactly the same with the other group. This prevented candidates being able to effectively organise, link, develop or evaluate opinions from the reading material. This aspect of the question is dealt with later in the report. Most responses were competently written in paragraphs. This was essential to the answers to all questions, but it was often disregarded in the responses to Question 3 , the descriptive essays. Most of the writing involved different stages or aspects of the topic. Therefore a sense of structure was necessary to show how descriptive details and ideas were linked. Occasionally there were long or unequal paragraphs in descriptions that panned across a scene, although short paragraphs could have been used to help focus on particular ideas that were reflective or most pertinent. Much of the writing showed evidence of thought and planning. It was advisable to think carefully and to provide at least a basic plan before writing responses to the composition questions. Both the narratives required a structure, with some sense of climax and a convincing ending, especially the second topic where it was important to consider the quotation and position it relevantly to highlight its significance. The two topics for argumentative/discursive writing required candidates to plan a series of varied ideas and arguments before writing. Question 3(b) in particular needed planning to avoid repetition and running out of relevant material. The best writing gave evidence of a wide range of appropriate vocabulary. ‘Appropriate’ meant that the language, particularly in descriptions, had to be precise enough to communicate pictures and feelings convincingly from the writer to the reader. Some of the answers contained language that was designed to show off vocabulary but it sometimes confused rather than enlightened the reader. Images were sometimes used that did not convey the unusual in terms that were either suitable or helpful. The best of the writing included few or no mistakes, but some otherwise good writers made a number of errors. Many of these were spelling mistakes of words such as ‘emissions’, ‘congestion’, ‘pollution’, ‘aeroplane’, ‘government’ and ‘environment’, words provided in the passage. There was still much confusion over ‘there’, ‘their’ and ‘they’re’ and especially, ‘your’ and ‘you’re’. Many sentences started with ‘also’. ‘And’ was overused to start sentences rather than used for special effect. There was much merging of words such as ‘alot’ and ‘atleast’. Many scripts had few or no punctuation errors, but some punctuation was inaccurate, particularly sentence separation (or ‘comma splicing’). Short sentences were frequently joined together because there was a relationship between them, but not a grammatical one. While there appeared to be less joining together of sentences with ‘then’, pronouns were used as conjunctions. It was important to correctly use commas, especially in longer sentences, to aid clarity of meaning. Greater care is required over the accurate use of apostrophes. The commonest grammatical error appeared to be the confusion of ‘amount’ or ‘less’ (of quantity) and ‘fewer’ (of number), particularly in Question 1 . In the writing of descriptions some responses needed to main control over present and past tenses and all ‘sentences’ required finite verbs. Those candidates who opted for the discursive essays, found the range of more complex tenses required in both these responses a challenge. Most of the handwriting was pleasingly legible, but some was very difficult to follow, leading to some words that were not decipherable. The paper asked for one composition only. There were no common rubric errors, but occasional scripts contained brief answers to one each from Questions 2, 3 and 4 . Section 1: Directed Writing
